newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Government accuses Islamists of ballot paper smear.
newsitem.headline: Government accuses Islamists of ballot paper smear.

text.p: Algeria's election campaign moved into high gear on Wednesday as rows broke out over copies of a ballot paper circulating in the town of Oran and threats by six parties to pull out in one constituency over alleged official bias.

Algerian polticians campaigned from far-flung oil and gas producing southern provinces in the Sahara Desert to violence-stricken mountain villages in the north in the fight for 16 million votes in the June 5 election.
The interior ministry accused the Islamist-leaning Nahda party of using a stolen ballot paper to try to cast doubt on the fairness of the election.

"It is obvious that this action was hatched in a clear aim of triggering a media fuss in order to arouse doubts about the authorities' neutrality in organising the parliamentary elections," said the ministry in a statement.

The statement said Nahda party officials, helped by a local government employee, had stolen one ballot paper and photocopied it many times and then distributed the copies in the streets at the western town of Oran.

Each party has its own ballot paper for each constituency, listing its candidates for the seats in that district. The stolen paper carried a list of candidates for the National Democratic Rally (RND), headed by party president Abdelkader Bensalah.
The party is widely recognised as being the main group for supporters of President Liamine Zeroual.

Opposition leaders seized on the incident, saying it showed the RND was getting direct support from the establishment. Some called on the authorities to change the ballot paper or arrange a by-election in Oran.

"The ministry insists that the leakage involved only one voting paper and reasserts its determination to apply the law on the instigators of this ill-intentioned action and their accomplices," the interior ministry said.
Nahda officials said they "have evidence proving their innocence and have proof which may incriminate other parties."

In another row, six political parties on Wednesday threatened to withdraw from the poll race in central Ain Defla province unless President Zeroual intervened to end what they called pressure and bias by local authorities.
They included the former ruling National Liberation Front (FLN) and Islamist-leaning Movement for a Peaceful Society.
Main political parties plan big rallies in cities this week to mobilise supporters by June 2, the start of a three-day cooling off period in which voters will reflect on their choice.

More than 7,000 candidates from 39 political groups and independent candidates are seeking seats in the 380-member National Assembly, being elected for the first time by a system of proportional representation.
The main battle appears between the pro-government RND and the Movement for a Peaceful Society (MPS), formerly known as Hamas. It was forced to change its name under a new law.
"They have taken from us 'Hamas' believing we will be finished. We put up to them the Peace and the RND lost its head," chanted MPS supporters at a rally in a working-class suburb in Algiers.

"Those who sawed off power pylons paved the way for those who cut the throats of the people," shouted RND backers in a separate rally refering to MPS leader Mahfoud Nahnah who turned from radical fundamentalist in the 1980s into a moderate leaning-Islamist.

The June parliamentary poll is Algeria's first since 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which the now banned radical Islamist Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had taken a huge lead. About 60,000 people have died since then in the violence that erupted.
